articles.title: Google Translate could soon get its own version of Gboard’s Rambler
articles.summary: TL;DR Google introduced Rambler for Gboard earlier this year, removing filler words and cleaning up your voice input for text conversion. Now Google Translate appears to be preparing its own similar mode called Smart assist. It’s not yet clear if Smart assist would have some of the same limitations as Rambler. Voice-to-text sounds like a great idea… until you actually listen closely to how people really speak. While we expect the written word to be clear and formal, speech is often anything but — and that’s exactly why we have tools like Rambler in Gboard , able to compensate for our messy utterances. articles.title: Surveillance Pricing May Be Coming to a Store Near You
articles.summary: What if the electronic shelf label you see at the grocery store isn't just showing you the price of the jar of mayonnaise you're about to buy — but actually raising the price because you put a can of tuna in your cart. It's called surveillance pricing and retailers like Walmart appear to be locking down technology that will help them figure out how much they can charge you. Bloomberg's Brad Stone joins Stacey Vanek Smith and Max Chafkin on the Everybody's Business podcast to unpack this pricing strategy (which Walmart has denied using). (Source: Bloomberg)

articles.title: The real reason your high-end Bluetooth headphones don’t sound as good as you’d expect
articles.summary: Credit: C. Scott Brown / Android Authority You’ve done your homework; you researched a pair of high-end headphones and lined them up with an expensive Hi-Res music streaming service, but something seems off. Your tunes just don’t sound quite as good as when listening with wired headphones or a speaker. The problem, almost certainly, is that you’re listening over Bluetooth — a convenient and almost unavoidable way to listen to music on our phones. I’ll spare you the history lesson, but the great irony is that Bluetooth was never really designed to transfer high-fidelity media between devices. The earliest Bluetooth audio specifications were designed for heavily compressed, mono-band speed, a far cry from the studio-quality masters that you can get your ears on today.
